strengths: SESaMo is a clean and practical mechanism for embedding both exact and broken symmetries (discrete Z_M and continuous U(1)) into normalizing flows, going beyond canonicalization which requires invariant priors, canonical-cell confinement, and equal mode weights.

The paper clearly identifies a real weakness of canonicalization: its inability to handle broken symmetries with unequal mode masses, and supports this claim both theoretically (App. E/H, breaking-ratio analysis) and empirically (φ⁴ theory with increasing breaking factor α, Fig. 12; Hubbard model with broken Z_4, Fig. 4).

The self-reparametrized KL divergence is a useful technical contribution: the derivation in App. J that the standard ELBO yields a zero gradient for the learnable breaking parameter b, and that the importance-weighted estimator term fixes this, is well motivated and correct as presented.

Extensive validation: benchmarks span a toy 8-Gaussian mixture, complex φ⁴ theory (unbroken/broken U(1)), real φ⁴ theory across a range of inverse temperatures and breaking factors, and the Hubbard model, with quantitative agreement between the learned breaking parameter and analytical predictions (Eqs. 39, 56) — a strong check that the mechanism captures the correct physics rather than just improving ESS.

Good reproducibility: code is released, hyperparameters are tabulated (Tab. 3), hardware, training details, and optimizer schedules are specified, and results are averaged over multiple seeds with standard deviations reported.
Honest limitations section (App. A) acknowledging the requirement of a priori knowledge of symmetry sectors and approximate bijectivity enforcement near canonical-cell boundaries.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is narrow: the paper only benchmarks against naive RealNVP and canonicalization. Stronger or alternative baselines — dedicated equivariant flows (e.g., the Z_2-equivariant architectures of Nicoli et al., or permutation-equivariant flows cited in related work), mode-collision/replica approaches for mode collapse, or simply a RealNVP with wider/deeper architecture and the modified KL objective — are absent, making the empirical case for the new mechanism less compelling than it could be.

The method is conceptually fairly simple: stochastic modulation is essentially a mixture over symmetry-transformed flow outputs, and the penalty-based bijectivity enforcement is heuristic (soft constraint, hyperparameters A and B tuned per task) rather than guaranteed; bijectivity can still fail when target mass lies near the canonical-cell boundary.

ESS is the sole quantitative metric in the main table, yet footnote 6 itself shows ESS can be misleadingly high (RealNVP reaches 0.88 on the Hubbard model while suffering mode dropping); additional observables-based validation is relegated to appendices and only partially addresses this.

Scale of experiments is modest: lattice volumes of 8×8 and 2×2 are small for lattice field theory benchmarks, and it is unclear how the penalty terms, canonical-cell construction, and the learned continuous-modulation map h(u) behave at larger volumes or for higher-dimensional symmetry groups.

The coverage of the claim that SESaMo handles 'a variety of exact and broken symmetries' is limited in practice: only sign-flip/rotation-type symmetries that decompose configuration space into disjoint sectors are tested; permutation symmetries and non-Abelian groups, which are common in chemistry/molecular applications, are not addressed or discussed in terms of feasibility.

The continuous-symmetry extension (App. F) is underexplored: the trainability and stability of the spline flow h(u), the choice of regularization γ = 0.5 for all experiments, and sensitivity to these hyperparameters are not ablated.

Positioning relative to work on mixture-of-experts / sector-augmented samplers in the lattice QFT literature could be sharper; the related-work section is thorough on equivariant flows but the novelty of 'redistributing mass across symmetry sectors at sampling time' versus prior mode-splitting tricks is not crisply delineated.

strengths: The paper is well-written and clearly organized, with an intuitive explanation of both the canonicalization baseline and the proposed stochastic modulation (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 5, App. B).

The proposed SESaMo method is simple and general: it can handle exact and broken discrete symmetries (Z_M) as well as continuous U(1) symmetries via a learned map h(u), which canonicalization cannot easily handle.

The self-reparametrized KL (Sec. 3.2, App. J) provides a clean derivation of why the standard ELBO yields zero gradient for the learnable symmetry-breaking parameter b, and how the importance-weighted partition-function estimate fixes this.

Experiments cover both toy problems (Gaussian mixture) and physically relevant benchmarks (complex phi^4 theory, Hubbard model), with quantitative ESS metrics, multiple seeds, training-time comparisons (Fig. 9, 14), and quantitative validation of the learned breaking parameter against analytical predictions (Fig. 10, 12).
Code is promised for release and hyperparameters/architectures are documented (App. I), supporting reproducibility.
Limitations are honestly discussed (App. A), including the requirement of known symmetry sectors and the sensitivity of the bijectivity penalty near canonical-cell boundaries.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea is conceptually simple—train the flow on one symmetry sector and then stochastically apply symmetry transformations T_i with a learnable probability to redistribute mass across modes. This is an incremental extension of canonicalization/equivariant flows rather than a fundamentally new technique, and the contribution feels thin for a top-tier AI venue.

Weak baselines: comparisons are restricted to naive RealNVP and the authors' own canonicalization implementation. None of the established equivariant flow architectures discussed in the related work (e.g., Kohler et al. [32], Boyda et al. [36, 57], Kanwar et al. [35], Schuh et al. [38]) are empirically compared against, even though Schuh et al. [38] is explicitly cited as the prior state of the art for the Hubbard model. The claimed 'new state-of-the-art' is thus not established against the strongest available methods.

Narrow experimental scope: lattice volumes are small (8x8 phi^4, 2x1 Hubbard) and the toy problem is a simple Gaussian mixture. There is no evidence of scalability to larger systems, higher dimensions, or domains outside lattice field theory (e.g., molecular data), which limits the significance and generality of the claims for a broad AI audience.

Methodological concerns: bijectivity of g_theta within the canonical cell is only enforced approximately via a penalty term with several hand-tuned hyperparameters (A, B) (Eq. 11, App. D), and the consequences of approximate bijectivity on the correctness of the learned density are not analyzed theoretically or empirically in a controlled way.

The continuous-symmetry extension (App. F) introduces an extra trainable map h(u) (a spline flow) whose expressiveness/capacity trade-offs, failure modes, and hyperparameter sensitivity are not studied; the treatment feels somewhat ad hoc relative to the discrete case.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on ESS; standard generative-modeling metrics, comparisons to MHC/HMC sampling performance, or observables beyond the breaking ratio are largely absent from the main text, making it hard to assess practical impact.

The scope of the 'self-reparametrized KL' contribution is modest: it is essentially replacing Z with an importance-weighted estimator to enable gradient flow into the Bernoulli parameter b—a known-style reparameterization trick—and its effect is not ablated independently of the modulation mechanism.

Significance for a general AI audience is questionable: the method presumes prior knowledge of the symmetry group and its sectors, and the benchmarks are physics-specific, limiting the paper's relevance and impact beyond the lattice-field-theory sampling niche.

strengths: The proposed stochastic modulation (SESaMo) is a simple, clean, and novel mechanism for embedding exact and broken discrete/continuous symmetries into normalizing flows, complementing canonicalization without requiring an invariant base density or a canonical-cell-preserving flow.

The self-reparameterized KL divergence with an importance-weighted partition function estimator is a sensible technical contribution, and App. J gives a clear derivation showing the standard ELBO yields a vanishing gradient for the symmetry-breaking parameter b, motivating the design.

Experiments cover a well-chosen progression: a Gaussian mixture toy problem, a complex phi^4 theory with broken/unbroken U(1), and the Hubbard model with a broken Z_4 symmetry, with quantitative agreement of the learned breaking ratio R against analytical predictions (Figs. 10 and 12), which is a convincing validation.

The paper reports results averaged over multiple seeds with error bars, includes wall-clock (GPU-minute) convergence comparisons, discusses limitations explicitly (App. A), and states code will be released with the supplement.
Writing and organization are clear; the comparison between canonicalization and stochastic modulation (Sec. 2.3.2 vs. 3.1, App. B) is well illustrated and helps position the contribution.
weaknesses: The baseline set is narrow: comparisons are limited to naive RealNVP and canonicalization. Missing alternatives for mitigating mode collapse in flow-based samplers (e.g., annealed/sequentially trained flows, non-equivariant mode-splitting schemes such as prior reparametrizations or MCMC-augmented training, and HMC as a reference sampler), which weakens claims of state-of-the-art.

The evaluation relies almost exclusively on ESS as the performance metric. As the authors themselves note in a footnote (RealNVP achieves high ESS on the Hubbard model yet fails to learn the target due to mode dropping), ESS can be misleading; no evaluation of physical observables with statistical errors, autocorrelation analysis, or comparisons against MCMC ground truth beyond density plots is provided.

The method presupposes that symmetry sectors are known a priori and that symmetry transformations map modes to distinct regions; the paper acknowledges this, but there is no discussion or experiment on how sensitive the approach is to mis-specification of the symmetry group or partially broken symmetries.

Scalability is not demonstrated: all lattice experiments are small (V=8x8 or 2x1/2x2), and the limitations section concedes that bisection-like boundaries of the canonical cell could degrade ESS in low dimensions; it remains unclear whether the approach helps on the larger lattices where sampling is genuinely hard.

Several design choices appear somewhat ad hoc and under-ablated: the penalty term with hyperparameters A and B, the fixed gamma = 0.5 in all experiments, and the extra learnable spline flow h(u) required for continuous symmetries (which changes model capacity relative to baselines) are not systematically ablated.

Conceptually, stochastic modulation is closely related to sampling a random group element and augmenting the flow output, which limits the perceived technical depth of the main mechanism; a deeper theoretical treatment (e.g., guarantees on mode coverage, bias of the KL estimator at finite N) would strengthen the contribution.
For the complex phi^4 theory, canonicalization 'could not be applied,' so the headline comparison on that benchmark is only against the weak naive RealNVP baseline.

strengths: SESaMo is a simple, well-motivated technique that extends equivariant normalizing flows to handle broken (not just exact) symmetries via a learnable symmetry-breaking parameter with a REINFORCE gradient estimator, filling a genuine gap in the equivariant flow literature.

The method is presented cleanly: the modulation construction (Eqs. 11-17), the bijectivity penalty term, and the generalization to Z_M, (Z_2)^N, and continuous U(1) symmetries (Apps. E-F) are coherent, and pseudocode is provided.

Experiments are reasonably broad and include physically relevant benchmarks (complex phi^4 theory, Hubbard model up to 18x100 lattices) rather than only toy problems, with sensible baselines (FAB, VMoNF, canonicalization) and multiple seeds with error bars in Table 1.
Quantitative validation against analytical ground truth (breaking ratio R for the Hubbard model and real phi^4 theory, Figs. 10 and 12) strengthens credibility beyond qualitative density plots.
Reproducibility is addressed with an MIT-licensed code release, hyperparameter tables, configuration files, and a stated LLM usage policy.
weaknesses: The key requirement that symmetry sectors be known a priori significantly limits generality; the paper acknowledges this but does not propose remedies, and the practical impact of this assumption outside lattice physics/chemistry is not demonstrated.

Bijectivity of the modulated map is only enforced approximately via a soft penalty term. The paper admits the ESS 'may decrease if only samples that strictly preserve bijectivity are accepted,' but never quantifies this bias; it is unclear whether the reported ESS values (which are the main metric) are inflated by invalid, non-bijective samples.

The method is essentially a symmetry-tied mixture over transformed copies of a single flow; the novelty relative to VMoNF and equivariant-flow mixture approaches could be more sharply delineated, and the 'for the first time' claim regarding learning broken symmetries is somewhat overstated.
REINFORCE-based estimation of the breaking parameter introduces high variance, and no analysis of estimator variance, bias, or convergence behavior of b is provided.

Evaluation is confined to a toy GMM and two specific lattice models; there is no comparison with stronger recent equivariant flow architectures (e.g., gauge-equivariant flows of Kanwar/Boyda on comparable tasks) or with established numerical samplers such as HMC, which the authors defer to future work.

Some benchmarks have questionable comparability: canonicalization cannot be applied to continuous symmetries and FAB is infeasible at the largest volume, so head-to-head comparisons are incomplete for the flagship Hubbard 18x100 result.
Minor issues: broken reference link for code (blank in the manuscript), typos ('continuos', 'estimating the correct breaking ratio'), and reference [61] is missing from the bibliography.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated problem: embedding (possibly broken) symmetries into normalizing flows for sampling unnormalized Boltzmann distributions, where mode collapse is a known failure mode of reverse-KL training.

SESaMo is a simple but sensible idea: redistribute probability mass across symmetry sectors with a learned categorical (or continuous) modulation variable, allowing broken symmetries to be learned—something canonicalization handles poorly.

Experiments cover a reasonable range: a controlled toy GMM benchmark with broken Z8 symmetry, complex ϕ4 theory with broken/unbroken U(1), and the Hubbard model up to V = 18×100, with both ESS and KL metrics, multiple seeds, and convergence-vs-training-time plots.

The learned breaking parameter b is validated quantitatively against analytical predictions of the symmetry-breaking ratio (Figs. 10 and 12), which is a convincing check beyond qualitative density plots.

A direct comparison with canonicalization (Schuh et al., 2025) on the same Hubbard setup shows higher ESS and the ability to learn broken Z4 symmetries, and code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core mechanism is a discrete/continuous symmetry transformation applied post hoc to flow outputs with a learned probability, which is an incremental extension of canonicalization and equivariant-flow ideas rather than a fundamentally new technique. The 'for the first time' claim regarding broken symmetries feels overstated given the closeness to prior work (e.g., Pires & Figueiredo's VMoNF, Köhler et al.).

The method requires symmetry sectors to be known a priori, which restricts applicability, and the framework for broken (Z2)^Nx symmetries uses categorical distributions whose parameter count scales exponentially with lattice size (b ∈ R^n with n = 2^Nx per the appendix), raising scalability concerns that are not discussed.

The bijectivity is only enforced approximately via a heuristic penalty term (Eq. 10) with two sensitive hyperparameters A and B; the paper acknowledges ESS degradation when probability mass sits near the canonical-cell boundary, but provides no systematic study of when this penalty fails or how to choose A and B.

Training relies on the REINFORCE estimator for the modulation parameters, which is known to suffer from high variance; no comparison against lower-variance alternatives (e.g., path-gradient or reparameterization-style estimators) or analysis of estimator variance is provided.

Baselines are limited to flow-based neural samplers (FAB, VMoNF, canonicalization, RealNVP). No comparison against established numerical techniques such as HMC is included—deferred to future work—which weakens the practical significance of the reported ESS gains.

Evaluation is confined to relatively small or specialized lattice systems; the complex ϕ4 experiments are on 8×8 lattices, and the generalization beyond hand-crafted physical symmetries (e.g., chemistry or molecular systems, where sectors may be less identifiable) is untested.

Presentation has notable flaws: broken links in the code availability and live-version statements, repeated typos ('continuos', 'estimated ration', inconsistent color coding between figure captions and legends in Fig. 10/12 where 'blue' and 'yellow' swap), and reference numbering issues (ref [61] missing).
Claimed contributions such as 'numerically enforce bijectivity via a penalty term' are framed as contributions but are standard regularization practice, inflating the apparent novelty of the work.

strengths: The proposed SESaMo mechanism is a clean and genuinely novel contribution: unlike canonicalization, it allows the flow to learn a single symmetry sector and redistribute probability mass across sectors via a learnable modulation probability, enabling—apparently for the first time—the accurate modeling of *broken* (both discrete and continuous) symmetries within normalizing flows, including a learnable symmetry-breaking parameter that agrees quantitatively with analytical predictions (Figs. 10 and 12).

The paper removes a key constraint of canonicalization (the requirement that the prior be invariant under the symmetry group) and provides a careful theoretical treatment: an equivariance proof for canonicalization (App. C), a well-motivated penalty term to numerically enforce bijectivity (App. D), generalization to Z_M, broken (Z2)^Nx, and continuous U(1)/SO(2) symmetries (Apps. E and F), and pseudocode (App. A).

Experiments are broad and physically relevant: a Gaussian mixture benchmark, complex ϕ⁴ theory (continuous U(1), broken and unbroken), and the Hubbard model at both tiny (2×1) and large (18×100) volumes, where the method scales to a broken (Z2)^18 symmetry and reportedly sets a new state of the art for NF-based sampling of this system.

Comparisons include multiple meaningful baselines (FAB, VMoNF, canonicalization, vanilla RealNVP), with ESS and KL metrics, multiple seeds, error bars, convergence-vs-GPU-time plots, and validation of the learned breaking ratio against exact analytical results for the 2×1 Hubbard model.
Good reproducibility: MIT-licensed code, archived version, hyperparameter tables (Tab. 3), configuration files, and a clear reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The core method is conceptually simple: learn one mode with a standard flow and apply symmetry transformations with categorical probabilities (whose Jacobians are typically trivial). Its novelty rests mainly on the learnable breaking parameters and the bijectivity penalty; the paper would benefit from a more rigorous discussion of how it differs in spirit from equivariant mixture approaches and from a theoretical analysis of when the REINFORCE-based estimation of b is reliable (variance, bias at late training when p_S → 0 or 1).

Bijectivity of S_u is only enforced approximately via the penalty term Λ, and the ESS figures may be optimistic if boundary-violating samples are not rejected; the paper acknowledges this but does not quantify the effect (e.g., fraction of samples outside Ω during/after training).

Baseline comparisons are incomplete in places: canonicalization cannot be applied to continuous symmetries, FAB is infeasible at the largest volume, and VMoNF is omitted for Hubbard 18×100; there is also no comparison against established non-ML samplers (e.g., HMC) which the authors defer to future work, making the practical significance of the reported ESS gains harder to judge.

The (Z2)^Nx construction in App. E.3 introduces a categorical variable over 2^{Nx} outcomes with n ≡ 2^{Nx} parameters, which would be intractable for Nx = 18; the actual parameterization used in the large-volume experiment (presumably per-site breaking parameters) is not clearly stated, and the scaling behavior of the method for large symmetry groups deserves clarification.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: citation numbering skips [61]; marker/color assignments are inconsistent between Fig. 10 and Fig. 12 (blue/yellow swapped); typos ('continuos', 'the the KL', 'estimation of physical observables... estimation' style errors, 'one a single A100'); and the live code link appears blank in the manuscript.

Evaluation is confined to physics-style benchmarks with known symmetries; the limitation that symmetry sectors must be known a priori restricts generality beyond physics/chemistry, and no experiment tests robustness when the assumed sector structure is wrong or only approximately known.

Claims such as 'establishing a new state-of-the-art' are made within a rather narrow niche (NF sampling of the Hubbard model), and the significance for the broader AI community rests on the assumption that mode collapse via symmetry modulation will transfer to other domains, which is not demonstrated.
